This $d$ represents the distance along the z-axis from the camera plane to the mesh surface [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that '$d$ represents the distance along the z-axis from the camera plane to the mesh surface'. However, the evidence explicitly defines $d$ as the 'eyespace depth' (or 'linear eyespace depth'). In the context of the provided text and standard computer graphics definitions for this technique, eyespace depth is the distance along the view direction (the ray), not strictly the geometric distance along the z-axis. Furthermore, the text distinguishes between $d$ (eyespace depth) and $|r|$ (true distance from camera to mesh), calculating $|r|$ using $d$ and the normalized ray length. While in a standard perspective projection the z-coordinate in eyespace often corresponds to depth, the text specifically refers to $d$ as the value sampled from the depth buffer and converted via `LinearEyeDepth`, which represents the distance along the ray in view space, not necessarily the orthogonal z-axis distance from the camera plane (which would be $z$ in eyespace coordinates, but depth buffers store non-linear values converted to linear depth along the ray). More critically, the text says 'The magnitude of d is the eyespace depth... d does not account for perspective' (referring to the raw buffer value vs linear depth) and later 'depth *= length(i.ray.xyz)' to get the true distance. The variable $d$ in the formula $|r| = d * |r_n|$ is the eyespace depth. The claim conflates 'distance along the z-axis' with 'eyespace depth'. In many contexts, eyespace depth *is* the z-coordinate, but the text emphasizes it is the depth *along the ray* derived from the buffer. However, the most direct contradiction is that the text defines $d$ as 'eyespace depth', and while eyespace depth is often synonymous with z-distance in simple terms, the text's derivation relies on similar triangles involving the ray length. A more precise reading shows $d$ is the depth value from the buffer (converted to linear). The claim says 'distance along the z-axis'. In eyespace, the z-axis points forward
